{{Short description|American mathematician (born 1941)}}
{{Use American English|date=August 2026}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=August 2026}}

'''Harold William Rosenberg''' (born February 19, 1941 in [[New York City]]) is an American [[mathematician]] who works on [[differential geometry]].<ref name="ABC">{{Cite web |url=http://www.abc.org.br/resultadoPT.php3?codigo=haroldr |title=Academia Brasileira de Ciências: Membros: Harold Rosenberg |access-date=2016-09-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160919164120/http://www.abc.org.br/resultadoPT.php3?codigo=haroldr |archive-date=2016-09-19 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Rosenberg has worked at [[Columbia University]], at the [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]], and at the [[University of Paris]]. He currently{{when|date=January 2021}} works at the [[Instituto Nacional de Matemática Pura e Aplicada|IMPA]], [[Brazil]].<ref name="ABC" /> He earned his Ph.D. at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1963 under the supervision of Stephen P. L. Diliberto.<ref name="genealogy">{{MathGenealogy|id=31509}}</ref>

In 2004 he was elected to the [[Brazilian Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="ABC" /> His students include [[Norbert A'Campo]], [[Christian Bonatti]], and [[Michael Herman (mathematician)|Michael Herman]].<ref name="genealogy" />

In 1993, he studied the hypersurfaces in Euclidean space with a given constant value of an [[elementary symmetric polynomial]] of the [[shape operator]], known as a ''higher-order mean curvature''. His primary result was to obtain some control of the height of such a surface over a plane containing its boundary. As an application, he was able to derive some rigidity results for complete surfaces with constant higher-order mean curvature.

In 2004, he and Uwe Abresch extended the classical ''Hopf differential'', discovered by [[Heinz Hopf]] in the 1950s, from the setting of surfaces in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] to the setting of surfaces in products of two-dimensional [[space form]]s with the real line. They showed that, if the surface has constant mean curvature, then their Hopf differential is holomorphic relative to the natural [[Almost complex manifold|complex structure]] on the surface. As an application, they were able to show that any immersed sphere of constant mean curvature must be rotationally symmetric, thereby extending a classical theorem of [[Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov|Alexandrov]].
